title: Part XI — PRACTICE: How Others Built It
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-13 from the published page (posts/part-11-intro/index.md, 367 words, nine units) and its former spec.md, then revised the same day (see decision_log). One spec paragraph per unit; the KEY POINTS callout carries the thesis; Figures 1 to 3 are evidence of the Kestrel & Pine paragraph (p04), after which they stand on the page.

know: Part XI reads four cases in order: Shopify (modularity, tenant isolation, checkout extensions and integration contracts), Amazon (services, cart design, fulfillment and the delivery promise), Zalando (team autonomy, shared API standards and later corrections, including a 2025 price-and-stock example where direct queries replaced a delayed event stream), and the composable movement (how its vendors' promises and offerings changed, and separate services added beside an existing platform).

How each case is read: public filings, papers, engineering posts and documentation researched on 7 November 2026; claims carry dates; older posts may describe replaced systems; unsupported internal explanations are labeled INFERENCE, NOT DOCUMENTED; each case ends with what the evidence could not establish.

Each company's engineering answered a different business and size, so copying its shape is The Giant's Boots; for Kestrel & Pine, with fourteen technology staff, the useful question is which practice helps its order flow and what operating burden it adds, and each lesson it takes confirms a Waypoint decision already made.
can_do: Say which kind of lesson from a large company transfers to a merchant of their size: discipline (dated API versions, reconciled integrations, one owner per fact), not machinery (pods, a hundred services).

audience.who: Readers new to commerce architecture (engineers, architects, product managers and leaders) who have read Parts I to X, or who hear 'Amazon did microservices' or 'go composable' in a design review and want to know how to read a company case and which kind of lesson transfers to a merchant of their size.
already_knows: What buying something online is like from the shopper's side; roughly what an API, a database and a queue are.

Parts I to X: the thirteen steps of an order, promise and handoff, the three status lines, system of record, single writer, events, idempotency and reconciliation; the failure-pattern names (The Giant's Boots among them); the four scale stages; the glosses for PSP, WMS, ERP, iPaaS, webhook, API call, SKU, channel, marketplace connector, 3PL and OMS.
Kestrel & Pine: a fictional outdoor brand with fourteen technology staff on a hosted shop platform, and the Waypoint program's decisions W1 to W8.
does_not_know: The four companies' records: each chapter owns its facts and sources; the page only names what each chapter examines.

Tenant isolation and Shopify's pods (glossed in a clause in p05: each shop kept apart in database pods); checkout extensions as Shopify uses them (owned by case-shopify; named only, as one of the chapter's subjects).

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the four cases in reading order, what each examines, and how the evidence is read.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the four chapters examine, in order, and how is the evidence in them read?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Shopify: modularity, tenant isolation, checkout extensions and integration contracts, separating older internal-architecture accounts from current product behavior, with version tracking and reconciliation as what a merchant adopts without copying the infrastructure. Amazon: dated accounts of services, cart design and fulfillment; reliable contracts, marketplace-held stock as a separate location and delivery promises computed from operations; where the evidence about today's internals ends. Zalando: team autonomy, shared API standards and later corrections, with a 2025 price-and-stock example in which direct queries replaced a delayed event stream for a particular need. The composable movement: how vendors' promises and offerings changed, separate services added beside an existing platform, and Kestrel & Pine's selective additions as the test. Evidence: public sources researched on 7 November 2026, every claim dated, inferences labeled, each case ending with what the evidence could not establish.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can say why a small merchant should not copy these companies' architectures and what it should take from them instead.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: why should a merchant with fourteen technology staff not copy these companies' architectures, and what should it take from them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each company's engineering decisions address a different business (a platform for merchants, retailers that also host sellers and fulfil orders, vendors selling services to assemble) and a far larger size; copying their shapes without their reasons is The Giant's Boots and adds systems to operate without a matching benefit. The documented record, read in the companies' own dated words, is narrower than the folklore and shrinks the slogans to rules a small team can use: discipline such as dated API versions, reconciled integrations and one owner per fact transfers; machinery such as pods and a hundred services does not. Each lesson Kestrel & Pine takes confirms a Waypoint decision already made.

thesis.question: What does the dated public record of Shopify, Amazon, Zalando and the composable vendors show about the book's argument, and which of their practices should a growing merchant adopt?
thesis.claim: The four cases' dated public records show the promises a merchant makes (price, stock, delivery date, refund) kept or broken at the joins between systems, and kept, between them, with contracts, one owner per fact, reconciliation and dated deprecation; each company in them sized its architecture to its own load, teams or customers. A growing merchant should adopt those disciplines, not Shopify's pods, Amazon's hundreds of services and delivery network, Zalando's thousands of applications or an all-composable rebuild.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the leading companies' architectures are models to adopt: Amazon and Zalando show that a serious commerce platform is built from microservices, Shopify that a modular monolith with enforced domains scales, and the composable vendors that the future is an assembly of best-of-breed services, so a growing merchant should move toward the architecture of the company it wants to become.
thesis.so_what: A merchant that accepts the claim answers 'Amazon did microservices' or 'go composable' in a design review by asking which documented discipline the example shows and at what size the company adopted the shape around it, and demands the disciplines of its vendors before copying any shape. Kestrel & Pine takes from the four cases lessons that each match a Waypoint decision already made (W1, W4, W5, W8) and changes none of its architecture; it declined the consultancy's February 2027 composable rebuild (about €3.2M, illustrative), a shape the composable vendors' own 2026 products no longer require.
thesis.how_why: Every merchant's systems meet at the same kinds of joins as these companies' (a webhook, a stock copy, an API version, a seller-of-record split), so the rules a company wrote for its joins work at any size: Shopify's webhook contract and Zalando's deprecation rules are written for any consumer of an API, however small. The shapes answered problems a fourteen-person team does not have: a front end that stopped scaling in 2001, 85-plus teams blocked by one codebase, millions of shops on one database fleet, enterprise customers with product-engineering teams. The companies' own later documents confirm this where a shape was corrected: Shopify's 2024 retrospective on domain boundaries, Zalando's 2025 move from events to a read API, the alliance dropping microservices and headless, commercetools selling modules for existing platforms.

supporting_claims.claim: A hosted platform's own record shows the change cadence a renting merchant must plan for: Shopify documents at-least-once, unordered webhooks whose subscription is deleted after eight consecutive failures, expects consumers to run reconciliation jobs, supports each API version for at least twelve months and withdrew checkout extension points on published dates, while its 2024 retrospective concedes that its domain boundaries did not match how its code works; the merchant adopts inventory, pinning, testing and reconciliation, not the pods or the renderer.

Amazon's record ties each move to a business problem: services after a front end that stopped scaling in 2001, a cart that accepts every add because a refused add is a lost sale, Prime and Fulfillment by Amazon opening its operations so that a third-party seller's item carries Amazon's promise while Amazon is not the seller of record, and investment in the network that keeps the delivery promise; the contract as the only door, availability for the cart but consistency for stock and payment, operability as a test for adoption and a computed promise transfer, while the network and the service count do not.

Zalando split its shop in 2015 for team autonomy, then narrowed choices for a decade and in 2025 replaced a price-and-stock event stream that lagged up to 30 minutes at Cyber Week and bred divergent copies with a read API; its written API guidelines on compatibility and deprecation, maintained in 2026 while its account-per-team platform tooling is archived, are what a merchant demands of every vendor, and events propagate change while a read API on the owner answers what a value is now.

The composable movement's 2020 promise did not say who builds the storefront or owns the joins between services; by 2026 its alliance had dropped microservices and headless from its principles, its own survey found 37% naming integration complexity a primary concern, and its vendors sold layers and modules beside platforms merchants keep, so a full assembly fits a Group-stage merchant with product and platform teams and an Omnichannel merchant adopts one owned capability at a time.

Read with dates and with documented facts kept apart from inference, each case divides into disciplines that transfer to a fourteen-person team (contracts, one owner per fact, reconciliation, dated deprecation) and machinery sized to the company; each lesson Kestrel & Pine takes matches a Waypoint decision already made, and each case ends where its public evidence stops, short of the company's current internals.

flow.rationale: Each case relies on what an earlier one established. Chapter 46 comes first for the reader's proximity rather than as a prerequisite of chapter 47, because Shopify is the kind of platform the book's merchant rents: its documented contract (webhooks, API versions, rate limits, dated withdrawals) gives the reader the yardstick for what a merchant can demand of any vendor, and its kept monolith sets the first answer to the monolith-or-services question. Chapter 47 then reads the company most cited for services and finds the move followed a scaling wall dated 2001, and that a retailer became a platform by opening its fulfillment and promise. Chapter 48 needs chapter 47: Zalando's 2015 split is read against Amazon's sequence with a thirteen-year lag and a different stated motive, its written guidelines as the documented form of the contract rule that Amazon's record holds only as a recollection, and its platform story as Amazon's in European form. Chapter 49 needs all three: the composable vendors sold to every merchant the services shape that Amazon and Zalando built for their own size and then corrected, and Shopware is judged against the hosted platform economics of chapter 46. Putting chapter 49 first would judge the vendors' pitch before the reader has seen what the shape cost the companies that built it; putting 48 before 47 would lose the comparison with Amazon's dated sequence that makes Zalando's motive and corrections legible; putting 46 later would open the part with a retailer's machinery, far from the renting merchant, and leave the Shopware comparison pointing forward. Swapping 46 and 47 breaks no dependency of chapter 47; its cost is that the part would open with a retailer's machinery before the reader has the hosted platform's contract terms that each later case is measured against.
